title: Smallest Largest Pile After Splits
statement:
You have piles of marbles; pile i holds piles[i] marbles. One split takes a single pile and divides it into two non-empty piles of any sizes you like.

You may make at most maxSplits splits. Return the smallest possible size of the largest pile once you are done.

examples.why: Two splits make three piles: 4 + 3 + 3. Halving the biggest pile each time gives 5, 5 and then 5, 3, 2, stuck at 5.
The 9 needs two splits to become 3 + 3 + 3 and the 4 needs one. Getting everything down to 2 would take six splits.
No splits allowed, so the largest pile stays as it is.

hints: Turn the question around: if someone names a limit s, can you say quickly whether every pile can be brought down to at most s?
A pile of p marbles needs ⌈p / s⌉ − 1 splits to get every part to at most s, and no plan needs fewer. Add that up over all piles and compare with maxSplits.
If limit s is reachable, every larger limit is too. Binary search for the smallest reachable s between 1 and the biggest pile.

explain.intuition:
Deciding how to split is hard: the first example shows that halving the biggest pile is a trap. Checking a given limit s is easy, though. A pile of p marbles must end up in at least ⌈p / s⌉ parts, and each split adds exactly one part, so it costs ⌈p / s⌉ − 1 splits. Piles do not interact, so the total is just the sum.

The check is monotonic: a bigger limit never needs more splits. That is the setting for binary search on the answer: search the range 1 … max(piles) for the smallest limit whose split count fits in maxSplits. It is the same move as picking the smallest chunk size that lets an upload finish in a given number of requests.
steps: Set lo = 1, hi = max(piles). The limit hi always works with 0 splits.
While lo < hi: let mid = ⌊(lo + hi) / 2⌋ and compute need = Σ (⌈p / mid⌉ − 1).
If need ≤ maxSplits, mid works: set hi = mid. Otherwise set lo = mid + 1.
pitfalls: Greedily halving the largest pile. Splits should cut piles into equal parts sized for the final limit, not in half.
Counting ⌈p / s⌉ instead of ⌈p / s⌉ − 1. The pile itself is already one part.
Writing ⌈p / s⌉ as p / s + 1. That is wrong when s divides p; use (p + s − 1) / s with integer division.

complexity.time: O(n log M) where M = max(piles)

solutions.title: Try every limit from 1 upward
solutions.idea: Check limits 1, 2, 3, … with the split-count formula and return the first that fits.

solutions.title: Binary search on the limit
solutions.idea: The number of splits needed only falls as the limit grows, so binary search for the smallest limit that fits.

followups: Each split now has to cut a pile exactly in half (rounding as needed). Does binary search still apply?
Return the actual list of splits that achieves the answer.
